steps: This video shows how one correlation I D lets you trace a failed request across separate systems. A claims request for policy A two nine four seven one reaches the A P I gateway, which mints the I D request a seven b two c nine d four and opens span one.
The gateway passes that I D in a header to the claims agent, along with the policy number. The agent logs the I D together with the exact model I D it is running, a Claude Sonnet four model.
Under the same I D, the agent asks retrieval to look up policy A two nine four seven one in the vector database. Retrieval records span two and returns zero results.
The agent logs the tool result, no matches, records span three, and responds to the gateway: policy not found.
Each hop exports its span to the trace backend. All three spans carry the same correlation I D, so the backend can group them.
Without that shared I D, these would be three separate logs in three separate systems, with nothing linking them to one request.
You query the trace backend by the request I D, and the three spans come back as one trace. The whole request is reconstructed end to end.

The trace points straight at the zero results from retrieval, and you find policy A two nine four seven one indexed with a typo. That is the root cause. Takeaway: mint one I D at the edge and log it on every hop. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
